title: Pea and Ham Soup
subtitle: Split pea soup with smoked ham hock
excerpt: Yellow split peas simmered with a smoked ham hock until the peas collapse into a thick, creamy soup, shredded with the pulled ham. Hearty, inexpensive, and deeply satisfying.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pea and ham soup is one of the great thrifty soups of British and Northern European cooking. Split peas were a staple winter food throughout the medieval and early modern period: they stored well dried and could be cooked with any available salted or smoked meat to make a filling, nourishing potage. The smoked ham hock provides both the flavour base and the protein. As the peas break down during cooking, they release starch that thickens the soup without any additional thickening agents. The soup is better the next day after the peas have continued to absorb liquid and the flavours have developed.

content.text: The ham hock needs a long, slow simmer to release its flavour and loosen the meat from the bone. Remove the hock from the pot once the meat is tender and pulls away easily, then add the split peas to the cooking liquor. Do not add salt until the end: the ham hock is salty and the soup may need none at all. The soup will thicken considerably as it cools.

Place the ham hock in a large saucepan. Cover with 2.5 litres of cold water. Add the onion, carrot, celery, bay leaves, thyme, and black pepper. Bring to a boil, skimming any foam. Reduce to a gentle simmer and cook for 1 hour 30 minutes until the meat is very tender and beginning to fall from the bone.

Remove the hock and set aside to cool slightly. Add the split peas to the saucepan. Simmer for 50 to 60 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the peas have completely broken down and the soup is thick.

Pull the meat from the hock, discarding the skin, fat, and bone. Shred the meat into pieces and stir back into the soup. Taste for seasoning: it may need no salt. Add pepper generously. Thin with a little hot water if it has become too thick. Scatter with parsley and serve.
